items.title: What do employers usually look for in hiring?

values: Materials and setup｜all fictional

A1: a fictional publisher asks for a 300—450-character children's story for readers aged 8—10; the theme is “apologizing after a misunderstanding,” and real children's data or existing story characters must not be used.

A2: the protagonist Xiao He mistakenly thinks a friend took the drawing book; the scene is the school reading corner on Friday. The factual clue is that the book was actually put into the art supply box by Xiao He.
A3: editorial feedback requires that the ending have the protagonist take the initiative to verify, explain, and apologize; the truth cannot suddenly be announced by narration.
Tasks and outputs
First write a one-sentence reader goal and a four-paragraph outline: misunderstanding, verification, discovery, apology.
Write a 300—450-character first draft, then revise the ending per A3; keep the before and after versions and list three specific changes.
Reference answers (do it independently first)
A passing outline should have Xiao He ask first, retrace the path of his own actions, find the book in the art supply box, and then admit the misunderstanding to the friend.
The revision notes should point out which sentence added a clue, which place changed the protagonist's action, and which place made the apology observable; existing stories must not be copied.

Sample fictional final draft (one example; it does not replace your own first draft and revision comparison): On Friday, Xiao He sat in the school reading corner, wanting to show the friend A-Qing the new train he had drawn. He searched his backpack, then looked under the desk — the drawing book was gone. A-Qing had just stepped away from the desk, and Xiao He shouted in a panic: “You took my book!” A-Qing stopped and said quietly that was not true. Several classmates nearby looked up, and Xiao He's face grew hot.

Xiao He reached out to open A-Qing's backpack, but then remembered that when he was organizing his art supplies that morning, the book had been squeezed in together with the long colored pencils. He pulled his hand back and first asked: “Have you seen it?” A-Qing answered: “I only picked up a blue pencil for you; after that you opened the art supply box.”

Xiao He searched his way back along his own seat, looking at the desk first, then pulling open the art supply box. The thick pages were pressed right under the colored pencils, and the cover still had the wheels he had drawn. He remembered that he had been afraid of creasing the corner, so he had stuffed the book in that morning, and had only ever looked in his backpack. A-Qing had taken nothing.

Xiao He carried the book over to A-Qing, his voice softer than before: “I put it in the wrong place myself, and I said you took it without checking first. I am sorry.” He also explained what had happened to the classmates who had looked over, without making A-Qing prove it for him. A-Qing nodded and handed him the blue pencil. Xiao He offered the chair beside him and asked whether A-Qing would like to help draw a road home for the train.

Three sample changes: add the “organizing art supplies in the morning” clue before the verification; change the action after the accusation to withdrawing the hand, asking, and looking back at the art supply box; and have the ending show Xiao He apologizing in person and clarifying what happened to the classmates who were watching. Because the original assignment provided no first draft, these three points are sample revision designs, and individual work must locate its own before and after drafts.
Boundaries and scoring

Five points: meets the character count and age range, the four paragraphs have clear causality, the clue is placed early, the apology is initiated by the protagonist, and a version comparison is attached; one point each; use only fictional characters and original text; the exercise is not a publishing contract, a copyright review, or employer hiring.
